questions.q: For square matrices A and B of the same order, under which extra condition does (A+B)(A-B) simplify to A^2-B^2?
options: C) A and B are both singular
questions.explanation: Direct multiplication gives (A+B)(A-B)=A^2-AB+BA-B^2. This equals A^2-B^2 exactly when the middle terms cancel, which requires BA=AB. Thus commutativity of A and B is the needed extra condition.

questions.q: Let A be an invertible 3x3 matrix and k be a nonzero scalar. Which statement correctly combines invertibility and the inverse of the scalar multiple?
options: C) kA is never invertible unless k=1
questions.explanation: Because A is invertible, AA^-1=I. Multiplying kA by (1/k)A^-1 gives I in either order when k is nonzero. Hence kA is invertible and its inverse is (1/k)A^-1.

questions.q: A and B are symmetric matrices of the same order. If S=AB^T-BA^T, what type of matrix must S be?
questions.explanation: Since A and B are symmetric, A^T=A and B^T=B, so S=AB-BA. Taking transpose gives S^T=(AB-BA)^T=BA-AB=-S. Therefore S is skew-symmetric.

questions.q: Suppose A, B and C are square matrices of the same order and AB=AC. Which additional fact is sufficient to conclude B=C?
questions.explanation: The equality AB=AC gives A(B-C)=O, but a nonzero matrix can multiply another nonzero matrix to give the zero matrix. If A is invertible, multiply both sides on the left by A^-1 to obtain B=C. Thus invertibility, not merely A being nonzero, restores cancellation.
